svg.title: Full tunnel, split tunnel and clientless remote access compared, and the four real risks that make split tunnelling a policy problem rather than a routing one
svg.desc: Top: three access models, each drawn as a path. Full tunnel sends all traffic through the enterprise, which gives the highest controllability because everything can be inspected, costs user experience because domestic browsing slows and video stutters, and fits highly sensitive roles and compliance requirements. Split tunnel sends only enterprise traffic over the VPN: the experience is good, controllability is medium because public traffic is uncontrolled and the endpoint may be infected, and it is the common practice. Clientless SSL VPN runs in a browser with no client, gives a good experience but low control because only published web applications are reachable, and fits partners, BYOD and temporary access. Middle: the four real risks of split tunnelling with their mitigations. The compromised endpoint becomes a pivot - mitigate with endpoint detection and compliance checks, and split by application rather than by address. DNS leaks because DNS goes local under split tunnel - send internal domains to the VPN resolver and keep public domains local. IPv6 bypasses the tunnel entirely when only IPv4 is tunnelled - handle IPv6 too, or disable it on the endpoint. Policy is bypassed when users can reach internal resources outside the tunnel list - keep ACLs on the tunnel side. Bottom: the warning that the split include list is a routing convenience and never a security control, because the enforcement has to sit on the headend.
svg.text: Remote access: the model decides who can be inspected, and the user decides the model
Every organisation ends up at split tunnel. The design question is what you did about the endpoint before you got there
FULL TUNNEL
all traffic goes through the enterprise
user
headend
internet
Control: highest - every packet can be inspected
Experience: worst - local browsing slows, video stutters
Fits: highly sensitive roles, regulated staff,
short-lived high-trust sessions
SPLIT TUNNEL
only enterprise traffic enters the VPN
user
headend
public Internet,
uninspected
Experience: good - this is why it always wins
Control: medium - public traffic is outside policy,
and the endpoint may already be infected
The trade you are actually making
CLIENTLESS · SSL VPN PORTAL
a browser, no client installed
browser
portal
web app
Experience: best - nothing to install, nothing to
keep patched on a partner laptop
Control: lowest - only published web apps are
reachable, and only through the portal's session
Fits: partners, BYOD, temporary access
SPLIT-TUNNEL RISK
WHAT HAPPENS
MITIGATION THAT ACTUALLY WORKS
The endpoint becomes a pivot
A user browses a malicious site while connected
Endpoint detection and compliance checks; split by application, not by address
DNS leakage
DNS goes local, so internal names fail or queries leak
Send internal domains to the VPN resolver; public domains stay local
IPv6 bypasses the tunnel
Only IPv4 is tunnelled; IPv6 reaches the Internet directly
Tunnel IPv6 as well, or disable it on the endpoint - pick one deliberately
Policy bypass inside the network
Users reach internal resources that are not on the split list
Keep ACLs on the tunnel side - never let the split list be the control
The sentence to keep:
split-include is a routing convenience. It tells the client which packets to send where; it does not decide what is allowed. Enforcement must sit on the headend.
Practical note:
if the split list must be "any" to make an application work, the application has an addressing or name-resolution problem, not a VPN problem - fix that instead.

Test before rollout: from an IPv6-capable home line, check that internal resources are unreachable when the tunnel is down, and that public traffic really does leave uninspected rather than silently through the tunnel.
